test: Send one short message saying sorry for something small you have not yet said sorry for.
note: Name the thing and stop there, for example: "Sorry I was short with you on the phone on Monday." No long reasons, no but. If there is nothing to say sorry for this week, send somebody a message saying you were glad of something they did.

test: Write down, in one word, how you feel right now, and one word for what would help.
note: Tired and a glass of water. Restless and a walk round the block. Cheerful and a song. The two words take ten seconds; looking for the true one is the exercise. A scrap of paper or the notes on your phone.

test: Tell one person one piece of good news from your own week, by message or out loud.
note: Small is fine: the tomatoes came up, you ran further, the car passed its test. Good news lifts the person hearing it too. If nobody is around, send it to the friend who always asks how you are.

test: Sing the chorus of one song you know, out loud, all the way through, twice.
note: Any song: a hymn, a football song, a song from school. The first time is to remember the words, the second time is to sing it properly, a little louder. In the kitchen with the tap running counts.

test: Write down three questions you would like to ask the oldest person you know.
note: For example: what was your first wage, what did your house look like, what did you do on a Saturday. Keep the list in your phone. You do not have to ask them today; having them ready is the step.

test: Pick the one job on today's list you least want to do, and do the first two minutes of it.
note: Set a timer for two minutes. Open the letter, find the form, fill the first line of the email. When the timer goes, you are allowed to stop, and often you will not want to. If today's list is empty, do two minutes of tomorrow's worst job.

test: Check every plant in the house with a finger in the soil, and water only the ones that are dry.
note: Push a finger in up to the first knuckle. Damp: leave it. Dry: water slowly until it just starts to come out of the bottom. No house plants? Give fresh water to a pet, a bird bath or a vase of flowers instead.

test: Walk up and down the stairs three times at a steady pace, holding the rail.
note: Not a race: steady steps, whole foot on each stair. Stop if anything hurts. No stairs at home? Step up onto the bottom step or a sturdy low step and down again, twenty times.

test: Guess the weight of three things in the kitchen, then check each one on the label or on scales.
note: A bag of flour, a tin of beans, a full kettle. Write the three guesses first. Most packets print the weight; a full litre of water weighs one kilogram, so a kettle can be worked out. Guess a fourth thing now that your hand knows more.

test: Set out everything you need for tomorrow morning in one place before you go to bed.
note: Keys, bag, the letter to post, the lunchbox, tomorrow's clothes on the chair. Then there is less to think about in the morning. If you already do this every night, do it tonight on purpose and count it.

test: Write a short note or message to a neighbour offering one small, real thing.
note: For example: "We are going to the shop on Saturday morning, can we get you anything?" or "Our ladder is free if you ever need it." Push the note through the door or send it. A neighbour you only wave to is a good choice.

test: Look up one saying in Irish or Ulster Scots and write down what it means word for word.
note: Search Irish proverbs or Ulster Scots sayings and pick one short one. Write the words, what each word means, and what the whole thing is saying. Read it out loud once, trying the sounds.

test: Sketch the view from one window in three minutes, using only straight lines.
note: Roofs, walls, the fence, the road, the edge of a tree: straight lines only, no shading. Set a timer so it stays a sketch. A pen and the back of an envelope is enough. From a room with no view, sketch the window frame itself.

test: Take two packets of the same food in your cupboard and work out which one costs less per 100 grams.
note: Look at the price you paid, or the receipt, and the weight on the packet. Price divided by weight, times 100. For example, 1 pound 50 for 500 grams is 30p per 100 grams. Many shop shelf labels already print this small at the side; next time you shop, look for it.

test: Send one person a message asking for one thing you could do better at work, at home or in a hobby.
note: Make it easy to answer: "What is one thing I could do better when we cook together?" Thank them for whatever comes back, and do not argue with it today. Asking is the part that takes nerve.

test: Bend slowly towards your toes with soft knees and hang there for five slow breaths, then roll up one bone at a time.
note: Let your head and arms hang heavy. Breathe out as you go down. Roll up slowly with your head last. Stop if anything hurts. Seated version: sit on the edge of a chair and let your chest fold towards your knees.

test: Draw the route from your front door to the nearest shop from memory, and mark three things you pass.
note: Arrows for turns, boxes for buildings. A post box, a tree, a lamp post, a gate: three things you would see. Next time you walk it, check which ones you remembered right.

test: Write three lines to yourself one year from now: where you are, what you are working on, and one hope.
note: Date it, fold it, and put it somewhere you will find it next year: the back of a drawer or an email scheduled to send to yourself. Honest and short is best.

test: Make a pencil look like it is made of rubber by holding it loosely and wobbling it.
note: Hold the pencil between thumb and first finger about a third of the way along. Move your hand up and down a little, quickly, and let the pencil rock. From a step away it bends. Try a pen or a spoon handle if there is no pencil.

test: Open a window for three minutes, stand beside it, and take ten slow breaths of the outside air.
note: Wrap up if it is cold; three minutes is all. Notice the smell of the air and the temperature on your face. If the window will not open, stand at the open front door instead.

test: Tell a child in your life one thing they did well today, and name exactly what it was.
note: "You kept trying with that zip and you got it" rather than "good boy" or "clever girl". Naming the effort is what they remember. No child at home? Send the same kind of message to a young relative's parent to pass on.

test: Clean the screen and case of your phone, and the keyboard or remote you use most.
note: A soft cloth, very slightly damp, for the screen; a dry one after. Tip the keyboard upside down and tap it gently. Wipe the remote buttons. Switch things off first.
